transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, to be honest, I guess I’m here because things have just been getting completely out of hand lately, especially at work. I’ve been an inspector on the line for years—checking parts, weighing samples, making sure everything is exactly up to code—and I’ve always been a professional. But lately, I just... I keep snapping at people. It’s like this sudden heat rises up in my chest and before I even know what’s happening, I’m just biting someone’s head off over the smallest little thing. 

Just the other week, we had this mandatory safety meeting. We all had to cram into the main breakroom, which is always too hot and crowded anyway, and someone was going over the new sorting protocols. And I just... I started yelling. I was practically screaming at them in front of everyone before I could even catch my breath and stop myself. It was so out of character, or at least it used to be, but in the moment I just felt so incredibly angry that I couldn't keep it inside. 

And now the fallout from that is just awful. The younger inspectors, the ones who just started on the floor... they act completely terrified of me. I see them whispering, and they won't even come up and ask me a simple question about a weight variance or a sample size because they're so scared I'm going to explode at them again. I hate that I’m making them feel that way, I really do, but I just can’t seem to stop being so angry all the time, and my supervisor suggested I come talk to someone before it gets worse.
Do you find yourself repeatedly thinking about or worrying over specific details or tasks outside of work?

Well, no, not really. I mean, I don't sit at home obsessing over whether a batch of widgets was weighed correctly or if the sorting machine is calibrated, you know? It's not like that. When I leave the floor, I try to leave the floor behind, although that's getting harder and harder to do these days with how wound up I am. But it's not the work itself that I'm worrying about. I've been doing this job for so long, I could do it in my sleep. I know the manuals, I know the tolerances, I know exactly what a bad sample looks like from ten feet away. So no, I don't go home and fret over the details of the job. 

It's more just... this general feeling I have. Like I'm always on edge, always waiting for something to go wrong, but it's not tied to a specific task at work. I don't go home and make lists or check things over and over. I just go home and... try to calm down, mostly. Which, like I said, isn't really working out too well for me lately. But as far as the actual tasks of being an inspector, no, I don't worry about those once I punch out. I just worry about... everything else, I guess. Or maybe nothing specific at all, just a constant hum of... I don't even know what to call it. But no, not work tasks. Not at all.
Have you noticed any changes in your personal relationships outside of work due to your recent behavior or mood?

Well, yes, actually. It’s... it’s bleeding into everything, to be completely honest with you. It’s not just the people at work, though that’s bad enough. I mean, I’ve missed so many shifts lately just because I can’t face going in, and when I am there, like I said, I’ve lost so much patience with the trainees. It got to the point where management actually pulled me aside and told me I’m no longer trusted to mentor the younger inspectors. Me! I’ve been doing this for years, I know the line better than anyone, and now they won't even let me train the new hires because I’m too unpredictable. That really stung. It felt like a slap in the face, but... I guess I can't really blame them, given how I've been acting.

But outside of work, it's just as bad. I used to be so involved in the local community theater. I’ve been doing it for, gosh, almost fifteen years now. I started out just helping with props and costumes, and then I eventually started taking on small roles. It was my outlet, you know? A place to just be creative and be around people who weren't talking about weight variances and sorting protocols. We were supposed to be doing a production of 'Our Town' this spring, and I was so excited for it. But I’ve had to completely pull back from it. I just... I can’t reliably get through rehearsals anymore. 

I’ll be sitting there in the auditorium, waiting for my cue, and that same tightness in my chest starts up. Someone will miss a line, or the director will ask us to run a scene again, and I just feel this overwhelming urge to snap. Or I just feel so exhausted and on edge that I can't focus on the script. I actually walked out in the middle of a read-through two weeks ago. I didn't even say anything, I just grabbed my bag and left because I felt like I was going to crawl out of my skin. My friends in the cast have been calling and texting, asking if I'm okay, but I don't even know what to tell them. How do you explain that you can't sit through a two-hour rehearsal because you feel like a coiled spring all the time? So I just stopped going. I told the director I had some personal things to deal with and stepped down. It breaks my heart, it really does, because I love those people, but I just can't be around them right now without ruining it for everyone.
Do you often feel anxious or on edge in social situations outside of your job?

Well, yes, but it's... it's a very specific kind of anxious. It's not like I'm worried about what people think of me or if I'm saying the wrong thing, you know? It's more physical than that. It's like my body just refuses to believe that I'm actually safe anywhere. 

Take the break room at work, for instance. I know you asked about outside of work, but it happens there too, and it's the exact same feeling. I'll be sitting there with my coffee, and instead of just relaxing, I'm watching the doors. I'm tracking everyone who walks in or out. If I hear a sudden machine noise from the floor—like a pallet dropping or a conveyor belt starting up with a clunk—I practically jump out of my skin. And I'm constantly checking who's moving behind me. I just can't stand having anyone at my back. 

And it's the exact same thing when I was at rehearsal for the play. We'd be in the auditorium, which is this big, old space with squeaky floors and heavy doors, and I just couldn't settle. I'd be sitting in the second row, supposedly going over my lines, but really I was just... scanning. Watching the exits. Listening to the stagehands moving set pieces around backstage, waiting for one of them to drop something loud. If someone walked down the aisle behind me, every muscle in my neck would lock up until they passed. 

It's exhausting. It's like my brain is stuck in this high-alert mode, constantly scanning for threats, even when I'm just trying to drink a cup of coffee or practice a scene about a small town in New Hampshire. I just can't turn it off. My body just... it won't let my guard down, no matter where I am or who I'm with. It's like I'm always braced for impact, just waiting for the next bad thing to happen right behind me.
Do you find yourself avoiding certain places or situations because of these feelings of being on edge?

Oh, absolutely. It's... well, it's actually become a whole ordeal just trying to navigate my day-to-day life, to be perfectly honest. Take work, for example. I go completely out of my way not to pass the main inspection bay now. I used to just walk straight through, right past the line to get to my station—it was the quickest way, it just made sense. But now? Now I take this ridiculous long way around, down the back corridor by the old loading docks, just so I don't have to even look at it or hear it. It adds a good ten minutes to my walk, and my supervisor even asked me why I was coming in from the wrong side the other day, but I just... I can't go near it. 

And it's not just the physical places, it's... well, the conversations, too. I absolutely will not talk about the accident if I can help it. People try, you know? They mean well, they want to ask how I'm doing or they get curious about what exactly happened, but the second someone even hints at it, I just shut it down. I'll walk away, or I'll talk over them, or I'll just flat out ignore them. I can't even stomach the thought of discussing it. 

It's even ruined things I used to really enjoy doing on my weekends. I used to go to these... well, it probably sounds a bit dry to most people, but I really loved them... these local industrial-history talks at the library. You know, learning about the old mills and factories in the area, how they used to run the sorting lines and the manufacturing back in the day. I've always found that fascinating, given my line of work. But I had to completely quit going to those, too. I just stopped showing up. The last time I went, the speaker was showing all these slides, these big blown-up pictures of old machinery—the heavy gears and the industrial presses—and... I just couldn't sit there. Seeing those pictures of the old machinery, it just completely set me off. It put me right back on that horrible edge you were just asking about, and I had to practically run out of the room. So, yes, I avoid the bay, I avoid the people asking questions, I avoid my history talks... I just avoid anything that might remind me, because I just can't handle it.
Do you ever find yourself reliving a particularly distressing moment from your past?

Oh, Lord, yes. All the time. It's... it's honestly terrifying how it happens, how it just completely ambushes me when I least expect it. I'll just be going about my day, you know, trying to mind my own business, maybe I'm just walking down a hallway or trying to sort some paperwork in a quiet room. And then, out of absolutely nowhere, something will set it off. 

It could be something so small, too. Just a sudden clank from a metal cart rolling by, or... or a smell. The smells are almost worse than the sounds, to be honest with you. If I catch even a faint whiff of hot oil—you know, that heavy, thick, greasy smell when an industrial machine has been running too hard and it's overheating—it's like the floor just drops completely out from under me. 

I'm not in the hallway anymore. I'm not wherever I'm supposed to be. That sound or that smell, it just puts me right back in that inspection bay. Instantly. And I can see it... I can see my coworker right there by the machine. It’s not like I'm just remembering it, doctor, it’s... it's like it is happening right in front of me all over again. I can see the exact way they were standing, I can hear the hum of the line behind us, I can feel that exact same cold, heavy dread in the pit of my stomach. It's so vivid, so real, that I've actually reached out my hand to try and grab them, to try and stop it from happening, right there in the middle of a completely different room. 

And it takes me so long to pull myself out of it, to blink and realize that I'm not actually there, that the accident already happened and I can't change it. I just end up standing there, shaking and gasping for air, because my brain completely convinced me I was right back in that exact horrible second. It just... it never leaves me alone.
